articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Awards £1.1 Million Contract for Young People's Accommodation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale. By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months. This initiative not only reflects the council's commitment to supporting young people but also highlights the importance of addressing homelessness in the borough.

articles.title: £150 off energy bills: Rochdale households urged to watch for important letter
articles.excerpt: Warm Home Discount confirmation letters are arriving for eligible households, with the £150 energy credit applied over the winter rather than paid to everyone at once.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents who qualify for £150 off their energy bills are being urged to check their post as Warm Home Discount confirmation letters begin arriving.

The government started issuing letters on Thursday, 22 October, with correspondence continuing through to January 2027.

Around six million households across Britain are expected to benefit this winter. The letters will explain whether the discount will be applied automatically or whether the recipient needs to provide more information.

Anyone whose letter asks them to contact the Warm Home Discount helpline must do so before 26 February 2027.

The Warm Home Discount supports eligible households, including people receiving qualifying means tested benefits. Eligibility depends on the scheme’s rules, including benefit entitlement and the electricity account arrangements on the qualifying date.

For this winter, the qualifying date was 23 August 2026.

The £150 is normally applied directly to an eligible household’s electricity account. It is not a cash payment into a bank account, and there is no single payment day for everyone in Rochdale.

Eligible customers should receive their discount by 31 March 2027. Residents can check their supplier’s app, online account or bill for the credit.

The scheme is separate from the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payments. Receiving the Warm Home Discount does not affect either entitlement.

For households watching every pound, the important step is to read the letter carefully and respond if action is requested.

Have you received your letter or seen the £150 appear on your energy account? Tell us your supplier and experience in the comments, keeping account numbers and personal details private.

articles.title: Rochdale projects £10.6 million spending on roads as repair programme targets borough streets
articles.excerpt: Council figures project £10.63 million in carriageway maintenance spending for 2026/27, around 26 per cent more than the previous year.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council projects spending £10.63 million on carriageway maintenance this financial year, around £2.16 million more than the previous year.

The figures appear in the council’s Highways Maintenance Transparency Report, which sets out how it maintains the borough’s roads and where the money goes.

Projected carriageway spending for 2026/27 is approximately 26 per cent higher than the £8.47 million recorded for 2025/26. The total includes £1.357 million in Department for Transport incentive funding.

The £10.63 million covers carriageway maintenance across the borough, including wider repairs and resurfacing. It is a spending projection for the full financial year, rather than a sum already spent.

The council’s capital programme lists 6.01 kilometres of road resurfacing and a further 7.10 kilometres of preventative treatment.

Named resurfacing locations include Whitegates Road in Middleton, Wordsworth Way and Seymour Street in Heywood, Belfield Lane, Kiln Lane and sections of Edenfield Road.

The report also records 10,998 permanent repairs and 364 temporary repairs during 2025/26, illustrating the scale of ongoing maintenance. Those figures count repairs rather than individual streets.

articles.title: From six modems to 580 staff: Rochdale’s Zen Internet puts people and planet alongside profit
articles.excerpt: Rochdale’s Zen Internet grew from £5,000 and six dial-up modems into a national broadband provider. Its B Corp approach puts customers, staff and the environment alongside profit.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale broadband business that began with £5,000 and six dial-up modems is highlighting how its B Corp approach shapes decisions about customers, staff and the environment.

Zen Internet was founded in 1995 after a conversation over a couple of pints between brothers Richard and Daniel Tang. Today, the company employs 580 people and supplies connectivity to homes and businesses across the UK.

Alongside that growth, Zen has retained its independence. Founder and chief executive Richard Tang remains its sole shareholder and has pledged never to sell the company.

What does being a B Corp mean?

Zen became a Certified B Corporation in 2020, joining a movement of businesses assessed against B Lab’s standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.

For Zen, that means considering the impact of its decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment alongside financial performance.

The company points to practical examples, including two paid volunteering days each year for every employee, a fully UK based customer service team and a Contract Price Promise offering no mid-contract price rises.

Its community support includes donations to charities chosen through staff votes, involvement in the Rochdale Ambassadors scheme to attract investment and support for Rochdale Circle, which helps older residents live independently.

Zen also says it reinvests profits in its network and services, uses 100% renewable energy and refurbishes routers to extend their working lives and reduce waste.

One sourcing decision involved choosing an alternative to planned solar panels after identifying modern slavery concerns in the supply chain, despite the additional cost.

A business built for the long term

Tang says the company’s independence gives it freedom to make decisions with lasting benefits.

“From the moment I started Zen, I wanted to build a company that made a positive difference to the wider world, not just the bottom line,” he said.

“Becoming a B Corp was a natural fit given our freedom to make long-term choices, like keeping our support team in the UK and never raising prices mid-contract, that a purely shareholder-first business might struggle to justify.”

For Rochdale, Zen’s story is also one of a locally founded company growing into a national provider while continuing to employ hundreds of people.

For customers, the practical questions are straightforward: how much will a service cost over the full contract, who will answer when something goes wrong, and what happens to equipment when it is replaced?

Zen’s approach puts those everyday concerns at the centre of its business story.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is folklore and what is missing from the archive? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, spells that cause a bridegroom’s death, a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is attested in contemporary court rolls or parish registers — lack contemporary documentary support. The story’s appearance in sources begins with nineteenth‑century collectors (Roby) and later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson as cited in modern guides); no contemporaneous medieval legal documents or parish entries confirming the prophecy or the precise characters named in the tale have been produced in those printed sources. In short: the prophecy belongs to the region’s oral and printed folklore tradition rather than to verified medieval record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

articles.title: Rochdale Wins Gold at Britain in Bloom Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale town centre has been awarded gold in the 2026 Britain in Bloom awards, showcasing the borough's commitment to horticulture and community efforts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale town centre has been awarded gold in the 2026 Britain in Bloom awards, triumphing in the Town and City Centres category. This recognition highlights the borough's dedication to horticulture and environmental responsibility, with Rochdale finishing ahead of competitors such as Floral Godalming, Shaftesbury in Bloom, and Sidcup Partners Ltd.

The judges praised the impressive floral displays contributed by Bowlee Garden Nursery, which played a significant role in Rochdale's successful entry. The town's submission included notable features such as the restored Grade I listed Town Hall, which received support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, and the Baillie Street Quarter, both of which reflect the borough's commitment to regeneration and community spirit.

Rochdale's victory continues the borough's success in the Britain in Bloom competition, following Middleton's win in the previous year. The town has a history of excelling in these awards, and this latest achievement underscores the collective efforts of volunteers, local businesses, and council teams who contributed to the beautification of the area.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed gratitude to all involved in the project. The win not only celebrates the hard work of the community but also aims to inspire further efforts in enhancing the local environment. With 44 finalists competing this year, Rochdale's gold award is a testament to what can be achieved through community collaboration.

articles.title: Planning Approved for New £11.4 Million Special Needs School in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has received planning permission to build a new special needs school, set to open in 2028, aimed at supporting children with complex needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has been granted planning permission to construct a new special needs school, designed to accommodate pupils with complex educational needs. The £11.4 million project will be located on a site off Mayfield Street and will serve as a satellite for Redwood School, focusing on children with autism and social-emotional challenges related to autism.

The new school will provide 64 places for students aged 11 to 16 and is expected to open its doors on September 1, 2028. The development will include a part one, two, and three-storey split-level building, complete with parking, play areas, and landscaped grounds. The aim is to create a secure and therapeutically informed learning environment that supports vulnerable young people.

Seven Architecture, the firm behind the design, stated that the facility will enhance the quality of special educational needs (SEN) provision within the borough. The school will feature a café and spaces designed to foster personal development and effective behaviour management, ensuring that staff can deliver specialist teaching in a supportive setting.

Construction is set to begin next year, marking a significant step forward in expanding educational resources for children with special needs in Rochdale. This initiative is crucial for local families seeking tailored educational support for their children, reflecting the council's commitment to improving SEN services in the area.

Plans for a 17-storey tower block next to the historic Marble Arch pub have been rejected by Manchester City Council's planning committee. The proposal, submitted by The McGoff Group, aimed to construct 153 flats adjacent to the Grade II-listed pub on Rochdale Road, which has been serving customers since 1888.

The pub's owners expressed concerns that the development would threaten its future, describing the proposed building as "overbearing and oppressive". Councillor Jon-Connor Lyons voiced his worries about the potential impact on "one of Manchester's distinctive and much-loved historic pubs", highlighting the importance of preserving the pub's setting.

In addition to the concerns raised about the Marble Arch, councillors noted the absence of affordable housing in the proposed development as a significant factor in their decision to refuse the application. The committee's rejection reflects a growing awareness of the need to balance urban development with the preservation of historical sites.

This decision is significant for local residents and businesses, as it underscores the importance of maintaining the character of the area while addressing housing needs. The Marble Arch pub remains a key landmark in the community, and its protection is seen as vital for preserving local heritage.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Generates Nearly £3 Million from Parking Fines Over Three Years
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has collected £2.88 million from parking fines since 2023, with the highest revenue year being 2025. The funds are reinvested into local road infrastructure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has generated £2.88 million from parking fines over the past three years, according to data obtained through a Freedom of Information request. The figures reveal that the council issued a total of 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) from 2023 to 2025, averaging just under £1 million per year. The year 2025 saw the highest revenue, with £990,256 collected from fines.

The total value of the PCNs issued during this period was over £5.6 million, although the actual income is lower due to successful challenges against fines and the costs associated with enforcing them. The council has stated that all revenue from PCNs is reinvested into the local road network, which may include repairs to potholes, road markings, and larger infrastructure projects.

The data also highlights the main hotspots for parking fines in Rochdale, with Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central, and Oldham Road Central being the locations where the highest number of PCNs were issued. The council emphasizes that these fines are not only a source of revenue but are also issued for safety reasons, ensuring that pavements remain accessible for wheelchair users and preventing blind spots at junctions.

This significant revenue from parking fines raises questions about the balance between enforcement and public convenience. Residents may want to consider the implications of these fines on local traffic management and safety. What are your thoughts on the effectiveness of parking enforcement in Rochdale?

This funding will support a range of initiatives aimed at celebrating the theatre's rich history and its impact on the community over the past five decades.

The anniversary project will feature an interactive exhibition and a digital archive, allowing audiences to engage with the theatre's legacy. Additionally, M6 Theatre plans to conduct community outreach projects that will collect stories from individuals who have been involved with the theatre throughout its history. This initiative aims to highlight the journeys of both audiences and theatre professionals.

Founded in 1977, M6 Theatre has made a significant impact on the lives of over 500,000 children and young people through its touring theatre productions. The anniversary celebrations will include a new youth theatre show, a community gala, and the commissioning of a specially made film and poem, all designed to enhance public accessibility and involvement.

The project will unfold over the course of one year, culminating in a celebration of M6 Theatre's contributions to the arts and education in the region. This funding not only marks a significant investment in the arts but also underscores the importance of community engagement in preserving local cultural heritage.

articles.title: Two Drivers Have Vehicles Seized for Ignoring Heywood School Crossing Patrol
articles.excerpt: Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

21:24 BST, 22 October 2026

Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.

Police in Heywood have seized two vehicles after drivers failed to stop for a school crossing patrol. The incident occurred when Mr. Jones, the crossing patrol officer, was already standing in the road as the vehicles approached. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during these incidents.

The vehicles seized included a moped and a silver Skoda. Police collected evidence, including witness statements, before taking action. This incident is part of a broader concern, as there have been 137 reported cases of vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols in the Rochdale area.

Councillor Williams expressed his dismay at the incidents, stating that such behaviour is unacceptable and poses a significant risk to children. In response to these ongoing safety issues, police have been using body-worn cameras in hotspot areas to deter dangerous driving.

The seizure of these vehicles underscores the need for increased vigilance and compliance with road safety regulations, particularly near schools. Local residents and parents are encouraged to remain alert and report any similar incidents to the authorities.

Published: 23 October 2026 2 irresponsible drivers who failed to stop for a school crossing patrol in Bury Old Road have had their vehicles seized by police. The incidents took place on Tuesday, 13 and Wednesday, 14 October 2026, with school crossing patrol, Barry, having to move out of the way to avoid the vehicles, a moped and a silver Skoda, even though he was already standing in the road. Fortunately, nobody was injured in the incident. The matter was reported to police, who used new powers under section 59 of the police reform act 2002, to seize the vehicles after collecting evidence, including witness statements. Cars and other vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols is a growing problem, with 137 fail to stops reported across Rochdale borough over the past 5 years. Body worn cameras are now being used in hotspot areas to try to deter dangerous driving and support prosecutions where needed. Councillor Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It beggars belief that somebody would see a school crossing patrol clearly standing in the middle of the road and continue to drive. Frankly I’m appalled. “We would like to thank GMP for their quick and decisive action and I think it’s a really good result. “We will not compromise on the safety of our schoolchildren, their parents and carers and our school crossing patrols. Being able to get to and from school safely and to be able to go about your job without fear is the very least anyone should have the right to expect. That’s why we will continue to report incidents to the police and to push for prosecutions wherever possible.” School crossing patrols across Rochdale borough have recently been issued with new coats which will make them even more visible as the nights start to draw in. Nicola Mcilvenney, the council’s school crossing patrol supervisor, said: “Our school crossing patrols do an extraordinary job and I’m relieved that nobody was hurt in these incidents. It could have easily been a tragedy. “We would like to remind drivers to be extra vigilant, particularly as it gets darker in the evenings. As soon as the school crossing patrol raises their stick, it’s time to stop. As we always say, slow and steady wins the race." Paul Clarke, traffic Police Community Support Officer (PCSO) team leader at Greater Manchester Police (GMP), said: “There are a number of offences related to failing to stop for a school crossing patrol, and, having considered all the circumstances here and looking at the evidence, we felt that seizure of the vehicles was appropriate. “School crossing patrol officers play a vital role in protecting children and other pedestrians and drivers are reminded that when a school crossing patrol officer displays the stop sign, all traffic must stop.” Related content Councillor Dylan Williams Council news from across the borough of Rochdale Road safety Was this page helpful? articles.title: New HMO Licensing Requirements Introduced by Rochdale Borough Council
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced new licensing requirements for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), aimed at ensuring safety and compliance among landlords.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has introduced new licensing requirements for landlords operating Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) within the borough. This initiative is part of the council's ongoing efforts to ensure that all rental properties meet safety and compliance standards, thereby protecting tenants and the wider community.

Under the new regulations, landlords must obtain a specific HMO licence for each property they manage. The licence is valid for five years, with a fee of £1,011 plus an additional £53 inspection fee per habitable room. This means that landlords with multiple properties will need to apply for a separate licence for each one, ensuring that all HMOs are properly regulated.

The council will conduct thorough checks to determine if landlords are 'fit and proper persons' to manage these properties. This may include a Disclosure and Barring Service check if initial assessments raise concerns. The licensing process aims to enhance the safety and living conditions for tenants residing in HMOs across Rochdale.

These changes are significant for both landlords and tenants in the area. Landlords must ensure compliance with the new licensing requirements to avoid penalties, while tenants can expect improved safety standards in their living environments. For more information on the licensing process, landlords can visit the Rochdale Borough Council's official website.

articles.title: Rochdale selected for £9.4m children’s mental health pilot
articles.excerpt: Breaking: Rochdale will join Stockport and Tameside in Care Together, bringing NHS mental health professionals into children’s social care teams from early 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has been selected for a new government mental health pilot designed to make support easier to access for children involved with social care and their families.

The Department of Health and Social Care has announced up to £9.4 million over three years for Care Together, which will operate across Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside.

Mental health professionals from existing NHS services will work within children's social care teams. The aim is to help families receive expert support earlier, with less difficulty navigating separate services.

NHS Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board will lead the programme alongside the three local authorities. It is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029.

Who could benefit?

The department says up to 7,000 children and young people across the three participating boroughs could be covered, alongside their parents, carers and guardians. That figure covers all three boroughs combined. A separate allocation for Rochdale has not been provided in the announcement.

The groups identified include children in need, those on child protection plans, children in care, care leavers and adopted children.

Support could include family therapy and help for parents and primary caregivers, with services tailored to individual needs.

What will change for families?

Mental health professionals will work within social care settings, bringing expertise into the teams already supporting children and families.

The government hopes this will make it easier to identify needs and arrange appropriate help before problems reach crisis point. Faster access is an intended benefit of the pilot, with its effectiveness to be evaluated during the programme.

Dame Diana Johnson, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety, said:

“For too long, fragmented mental health services have left young people in care, care leavers, parents, carers, and guardians not knowing where to turn for support.

“We are committed to change how we support young people, and this exciting and innovative pilot will see thousands more children across Greater Manchester get specialist mental health support based on their personal needs and in quicker time, before they reach crisis point.”

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said children supported by social care can face severe mental health challenges because of trauma and adversity. He said the pilot forms part of wider efforts to support vulnerable young people as they move into adult life.

Professor Manisha Kumar, Chief Clinical Officer at NHS Greater Manchester, said the programme would help partners provide earlier support that takes account of children's experiences and wider family circumstances.

She said learning from the work in Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside would also help shape changes nationally.

When will Care Together start?

The pilot is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029. An evaluation will assess whether the approach could be extended to other parts of the country.

The announcement does not yet specify how many Rochdale families will receive support, how referrals will work or which local teams will take part.

For local families, those practical details will matter: who can access help, how quickly it becomes available and whether bringing services together makes support easier to obtain.

What would make the biggest difference to mental health support for children and families in Rochdale? Share your thoughts in the comments, while protecting children's privacy and avoiding details that could identify them.

articles.title: Volunteers urgently needed at Hollingworth Lake to help Rochdale Sea Cadets
articles.excerpt: GTAS is appealing for volunteers and a donated skip to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets on Saturday 24 October, meeting at 10am.
articles.content_html:
GTAS has issued an urgent appeal for volunteers to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets this Saturday, 24 October.

Anyone able to lend a hand is asked to meet at Hollingworth Lake council car park at 10am. Organisers say help would be welcome for any length of time, whether volunteers can spare an hour or stay for the day.

The group describes the clearance as a big task and is asking people to bring sturdy gardening gloves if they have them. Spades, shovels, loppers, other gardening tools and wheelbarrows would also be useful.

Local businesses are being asked to support the effort too. GTAS is looking for a skip or waste company willing to donate a skip for a few hours to help with the clearance.

The volunteer day is an opportunity for residents and businesses to give practical support to Rochdale Sea Cadets by helping bring the overgrown space back into use.

Anyone who can volunteer or help provide a skip should message GTAS directly through the group’s appeal post.

Could you spare an hour on Saturday, or do you know a business that could help? Share the appeal and let us know your thoughts in the comments.
